passage:
The Great Depression of the 1930s produced not one but several competing interpretations, each reflecting different assumptions about how market economies operate. The monetarist account, associated above all with Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, locates the catastrophe primarily in the actions of the Federal Reserve: by permitting a catastrophic contraction in the money supply between 1929 and 1933—a reduction of roughly one-third—the Fed transformed a manageable recession into a decade-long slump. On this account, the Depression was not an indictment of capitalism per se but of monetary mismanagement by a central institution that failed to act as a lender of last resort.

But the economist Barry Eichengreen challenges the Friedman-Schwartz narrative, arguing that it assigns excessive causal weight to domestic monetary policy and too little to the international architecture of the time. Eichengreen contends that the gold standard—the arrangement under which currencies were pegged to gold at fixed rates—was the structural mechanism that transmitted financial distress across national borders and prevented individual governments from responding effectively. Under gold-standard rules, a country facing a run on its currency could not freely expand its money supply without risking the exhaustion of its gold reserves. This constraint, Eichengreen argues, forced policymakers in country after country into deflationary policies that deepened and prolonged the slump even as domestic conditions were crying out for stimulus. Crucially, those countries that abandoned the gold standard earliest—Britain in 1931, the United States in 1933, France only in 1936—recovered earliest, a correlation Eichengreen regards as close to causal.

A third line of interpretation, developed by the economic historian Christina Romer, questions both accounts on empirical grounds. Romer argues that the standard statistical series used by both Friedman-Schwartz and Eichengreen to measure pre-Depression output were themselves artifacts of flawed methodology—specifically, that pre-1929 data were constructed using techniques that systematically overstated interwar volatility. When the series are corrected, Romer finds, the Depression appears slightly less dramatic in its initial drop, but the recovery turns out to be substantially more modest than conventional accounts suggest: the economy had not returned to trend by the time World War II effectively ended the debate. This reinterpretation cuts against the Friedman-Schwartz story, which presupposes a sharp V-shaped contraction and recovery, but it also complicates Eichengreen's optimism about early gold-standard exit, since the recoveries Eichengreen traces may be partly statistical artefacts.

These debates are not merely historiographical. The relative weight assigned to monetary policy, international institutions, and measurement uncertainty carries direct implications for how economists model financial crises today. If Friedman and Schwartz are broadly correct, central-bank intervention is the decisive lever; if Eichengreen is correct, the design of international monetary architecture may matter as much; and if Romer is correct, humility about the quality of available data should temper both sets of policy prescriptions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Friedman-Schwartz account of the Great Depression has been largely discredited by subsequent research into international monetary institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three competing scholarly interpretations of the Great Depression differ on the relative importance of monetary policy, international institutions, and data quality, and those differences carry ongoing implications for economic policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Christina Romer's revision of pre-Depression statistical series undermines both the Friedman-Schwartz and Eichengreen accounts and should be regarded as the most authoritative interpretation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gold standard was the single most important cause of the Great Depression because it prevented individual governments from expanding their money supplies in response to financial distress.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Debates among economists about the causes of the Great Depression demonstrate that historical statistics are too unreliable to support confident causal claims.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces three accounts (Friedman-Schwartz, Eichengreen, Romer), carefully describes each, and closes by linking their differences to present-day policy stakes — exactly what B captures.
explanations.A: Too narrow and too strong: the passage does not say the Friedman-Schwartz account has been 'largely discredited'; Romer complicates it but does not refute it outright.
explanations.C: The passage does not elevate Romer above the other two; it presents all three as live competing interpretations.
explanations.D: This restates Eichengreen's view as if it were the author's conclusion; the author remains analytic rather than endorsing any single account.
explanations.E: Too narrow: statistical unreliability is Romer's contribution, not the passage's overall thesis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the three interpretations of the Great Depression discussed in the passage can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of Romer's reinterpretation over the earlier monetarist and international accounts

choices.label: B
choices.text: equal skepticism toward all three, on the grounds that historical data about the Depression are irretrievably flawed

choices.label: C
choices.text: analytical evenhandedness, presenting each account's explanatory logic and its limitations without declaring any one definitive

choices.label: D
choices.text: implicit support for Eichengreen's gold-standard thesis, as evidenced by the greater length of its presentation

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarded skepticism toward all empirical claims about the Depression, suggesting that the topic is inherently unsuitable for economic modeling

explanations.correct: The author describes each interpretation in neutral reporting language ('argues,' 'contends,' 'finds'), presents limitations of each, and draws no explicit evaluative conclusion — a posture of analytic evenhandedness.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse Romer; he presents her findings as a complication that affects multiple accounts.
explanations.B: The author does not express 'equal skepticism'; he takes the evidence of each seriously.
explanations.D: Length of treatment does not imply endorsement; the passage devotes comparable space to all three.
explanations.E: The closing paragraph explicitly affirms that the debates have direct implications for modeling financial crises today, contradicting the idea that the topic is unsuitable for modeling.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A widely accepted interpretation is presented, a competing interpretation is described, and both are then rejected in favor of a third account that the author endorses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A puzzle is posed about the causes of the Great Depression, one interpretation is offered, a second interpretation challenges the first on structural grounds, a third challenges both on empirical grounds, and the broader significance of the debate is noted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Three interpretations of the Great Depression are described, the methodological weaknesses of each are catalogued, and the passage concludes that no reliable interpretation is possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historical episode is introduced, two competing causal accounts are compared, and a synthesis reconciling both accounts is developed in the final paragraph.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dominant scholarly consensus is described, its empirical basis is questioned, and a reformed version of the consensus is proposed as a replacement.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the monetarist account; paragraph 2 presents Eichengreen's structural challenge; paragraph 3 introduces Romer's empirical challenge to both; paragraph 4 notes the policy implications. B tracks all four moves in order.
explanations.A: The author does not reject the first two accounts in favor of the third; Romer complicates but does not replace them.
explanations.C: The passage does not catalogue the weaknesses of all three, and it does not conclude that no interpretation is possible.
explanations.D: No synthesis is developed; the closing paragraph notes stakes without reconciling the accounts.
explanations.E: There is no single 'dominant consensus' that is questioned; three distinct accounts are presented serially.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Eichengreen regards which one of the following as evidence that the gold standard played a causal role in prolonging the Great Depression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Federal Reserve allowed the money supply to contract by roughly one-third between 1929 and 1933.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pre-1929 statistical series were constructed using methods that overstated interwar economic volatility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries that abandoned the gold standard at an earlier date recovered from the Depression at an earlier date.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gold-standard rules required that currency reserves be maintained at fixed nominal levels regardless of domestic conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: France's delayed exit from the gold standard in 1936 was attributable to political rather than economic considerations.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that countries abandoning the gold standard earliest — Britain in 1931, the US in 1933, France only in 1936 — recovered earliest, and that Eichengreen regards this correlation as 'close to causal.'
explanations.A: This is the Friedman-Schwartz finding, not Eichengreen's evidence.
explanations.B: This is Romer's empirical point about flawed statistical methodology.
explanations.D: The passage says gold-standard rules prevented free money-supply expansion; it does not say reserves had to be maintained at fixed nominal levels — an altered-detail trap.
explanations.E: The passage mentions France's 1936 exit as a data point but attributes no political explanation to it.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that if Romer's statistical corrections are accepted, which one of the following would follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Friedman-Schwartz account becomes the most defensible of the three interpretations, since it does not rely on pre-1929 data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither the sharp contraction implied by Friedman and Schwartz nor the robust early recoveries Eichengreen identifies would be fully supported by the data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Great Depression would be reclassified as a series of moderate recessions rather than a single catastrophic downturn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International monetary architecture would be shown to be irrelevant to the severity of the Depression.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Central-bank intervention would emerge as the only reliable policy tool for preventing future financial crises.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Romer's corrections undercut the 'V-shaped contraction and recovery' presupposed by Friedman-Schwartz and also compromise Eichengreen's optimism about early gold-standard exit, since those recoveries may be partly statistical artefacts — making B a direct inference.
explanations.A: The passage says Romer's corrections cut against the Friedman-Schwartz story; they are not exonerated.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest the Depression would be reclassified as moderate recessions; it simply appears 'slightly less dramatic in its initial drop' while the recovery appears 'more modest.'
explanations.D: Romer's corrections complicate Eichengreen but do not demonstrate that international architecture is irrelevant.
explanations.E: No such conclusion follows from Romer's work; this conflates Romer's empirical revision with a policy prescription the passage attributes to the Friedman-Schwartz camp.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely includes the specific years of gold-standard abandonment (Britain in 1931, the United States in 1933, France only in 1936) in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that different countries had different political cultures that affected their willingness to break international monetary rules

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide the concrete chronological sequence that grounds Eichengreen's claim that timing of gold-standard exit correlates with timing of recovery

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the United States was the pivotal actor whose monetary decisions determined outcomes for all other economies

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that Friedman and Schwartz were correct to focus on domestic Federal Reserve policy rather than international monetary arrangements

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the empirical material that Romer later argues is statistically unreliable

explanations.correct: The years are presented immediately after the claim that countries abandoning the gold standard earliest recovered earliest — they are the specific evidence for that correlational claim, grounding Eichengreen's near-causal inference.
explanations.A: The passage makes no reference to political culture; this imports a concept not in the text.
explanations.C: The passage does not single out the United States as pivotal; all three countries are listed as illustrative cases.
explanations.D: The dates are in Eichengreen's section and support his international account, not Friedman-Schwartz's domestic one.
explanations.E: Romer's statistical critique concerns pre-1929 data series, not the gold-standard abandonment dates from 1931–1936.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine Eichengreen's argument that abandoning the gold standard caused early economic recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several countries that remained on the gold standard throughout the 1930s experienced deeper recessions than countries that exited early.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Britain's 1931 gold-standard exit was preceded by a series of domestic fiscal stimulus measures that could independently account for its subsequent recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Federal Reserve's contraction of the money supply was more severe in absolute terms than the deflationary pressures created by gold-standard rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: France experienced a more severe depression between 1931 and 1936 than either Britain or the United States during those same years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economists today largely agree that both monetary policy and international architecture contributed to the severity of the Great Depression.

explanations.correct: Eichengreen's argument depends on exit from the gold standard being the causal mechanism of recovery. If Britain had implemented independent fiscal stimulus measures before its exit, those measures — not the exit itself — could explain its recovery, breaking the causal chain Eichengreen posits.
explanations.A: This would actually support Eichengreen's claim, not undermine it.
explanations.C: This is relevant to the Friedman-Schwartz vs. Eichengreen comparison but does not directly undermine the causal claim that gold-standard exit caused recovery.
explanations.D: France's worse outcome while on the gold standard is consistent with Eichengreen's thesis and would tend to support rather than undermine it.
explanations.E: A present-day consensus acknowledging multiple causes does not specifically undermine the gold-standard-exit-causes-recovery causal claim.

passage:
The study of collective memory — the way groups selectively recall, narrate, and institutionalize the past — has been shaped by a long-running debate between two intellectual traditions. The first, associated with the sociologist Maurice Halbwachs, holds that memory is irreducibly social: individuals can remember only what is sanctioned by the groups to which they belong, and the frameworks through which the past is apprehended are always collective frameworks. On this view, there is no such thing as genuinely personal memory, because even the most intimate recollection is shaped by language, narrative convention, and social expectation.

Halbwachs's framework attracted powerful criticism from the historian Pierre Nora, who argued that the rise of modernity had introduced a fateful rupture between living memory — the spontaneous, unself-conscious transmission of the past within communities — and what Nora called lieux de mémoire, or 'sites of memory': archives, monuments, commemorations, and other manufactured substitutes for the organic tradition that modernity had destroyed. For Nora, the proliferation of such sites is itself a symptom of memory's death; we resort to archival memory precisely because living memory has been evacuated. The melancholy irony Nora identified is that the very institutions designed to preserve the past accelerate the forgetting of the lived experience they claim to commemorate.

A third position, developed by the social psychologist James Wertsch, draws on both traditions while resisting their conclusions. Wertsch agrees with Halbwachs that memory is mediated by collective cultural tools — above all, narratives — but he resists the implication that individual agency is thereby eliminated. Wertsch distinguishes between mastery of a narrative, which means being able to reproduce it accurately, and appropriation, which means internalizing the narrative as genuinely one's own. In the societies Wertsch has studied most closely — particularly post-Soviet Russia — he finds that citizens often master official national narratives about, say, the Second World War without appropriating them: they can recite the narrative fluently while remaining emotionally detached or even privately skeptical. This split between mastery and appropriation is, for Wertsch, the key to understanding both the resilience of official memory cultures and the possibility of resistance to them.

Wertsch's framework has important methodological consequences. Survey research that asks respondents to agree or disagree with official historical claims will capture mastery without touching appropriation; the same answer can conceal radically different relationships to the narrative. What looks like broad consensus in opinion data may mask a population that has learned to perform a narrative while privately maintaining alternative versions of the past. Historians and social scientists who rely solely on such data, Wertsch implies, risk systematically misreading the societies they study — a caution that applies with particular force in authoritarian or post-authoritarian contexts where the performance of official memory is socially mandatory.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is most likely to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that Wertsch's distinction between mastery and appropriation is the definitive solution to the problem of collective memory

choices.label: B
choices.text: trace the evolution of scholarly thinking about collective memory through three positions, culminating in an account that has significant methodological implications for social research

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that Halbwachs's and Nora's accounts of collective memory are fundamentally incompatible with each other

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why modern societies have constructed ever-greater numbers of memorial sites, archives, and commemorative institutions

choices.label: E
choices.text: evaluate the adequacy of survey research as a tool for studying historical consciousness in authoritarian societies

explanations.correct: The passage moves through Halbwachs, then Nora (who challenges Halbwachs), then Wertsch (who synthesizes and extends both), and closes by drawing out the methodological stakes of Wertsch's view — a trajectory that B captures faithfully.
explanations.A: The author presents Wertsch's view approvingly but does not declare it a 'definitive solution'; this overstates the author's endorsement.
explanations.C: The passage does not characterize Halbwachs and Nora as 'fundamentally incompatible'; Nora is presented as a critic of Halbwachs, not as operating from an incommensurable framework.
explanations.D: This restates Nora's thesis, which is only one paragraph of the passage and not the passage's primary purpose.
explanations.E: Survey research is mentioned only in the final paragraph as a specific application; it is not the primary subject of the passage.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following best captures what Halbwachs meant by claiming that memory is 'irreducibly social'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individuals are biologically incapable of forming long-term memories without reinforcement from social groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even personal recollections are structured by the collective frameworks — language, narrative, social expectation — sanctioned by the groups to which the rememberer belongs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Memory is shaped primarily by official government institutions, which determine which events will be commemorated and which forgotten.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reliability of any given memory can only be assessed by comparing it against the recollections of other members of the same social group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Communities form memories collectively through ritual and ceremony, but individuals retain the capacity to remember privately and independently.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that on Halbwachs's view, 'even the most intimate recollection is shaped by language, narrative convention, and social expectation,' and that individuals can remember only what is sanctioned by their groups — B paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: The passage makes no biological claim; the argument is sociological, not neurological.
explanations.C: Halbwachs's 'social frameworks' are broader than government institutions — the passage attributes the institutional account of sites of memory to Nora, not Halbwachs.
explanations.D: The passage does not say Halbwachs located reliability in cross-individual comparison; this is a plausible-sounding detail not in the text.
explanations.E: This directly contradicts Halbwachs's claim that there is 'no such thing as genuinely personal memory.'

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that Nora would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Archives and monuments are the most reliable instruments for preserving authentic historical experience across generations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The construction of memorials and commemorative sites is a sign that the living transmission of shared experience within communities has already been lost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modernity strengthened living memory by giving communities new institutional tools for transmitting the past.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Halbwachs was correct that memory is irreducibly social, but failed to account for the disruptions introduced by industrialization.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proliferation of official memory sites in post-authoritarian societies reflects a healthy collective effort to reckon with a difficult past.

explanations.correct: Nora argues that 'sites of memory' are manufactured substitutes that proliferate precisely because living memory has been evacuated by modernity — making their proliferation a symptom, not a solution. B captures this inference directly.
explanations.A: Nora takes the opposite view: archives substitute for living memory but do not preserve authentic experience; the passage calls this a 'melancholy irony.'
explanations.C: This inverts Nora's argument; he holds that modernity destroyed living memory rather than strengthening it.
explanations.D: The passage does not say Nora endorsed Halbwachs's framework while extending it to industrialization; Nora is presented as a distinct critic, not a Halbwachsian.
explanations.E: Nora's theory is not limited to authoritarian societies, and the passage characterizes his view as melancholic — the opposite of 'healthy collective effort.'

questions.questionStem: The passage states that in post-Soviet Russia, Wertsch found that citizens often

choices.label: A
choices.text: appropriated official narratives about the Second World War as genuinely their own while publicly questioning them

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejected official national narratives in favor of alternative accounts transmitted through family memory

choices.label: C
choices.text: could reproduce official narratives about the Second World War accurately while remaining emotionally detached or privately skeptical

choices.label: D
choices.text: displayed both mastery and appropriation of official narratives, confirming the effectiveness of state memory institutions

choices.label: E
choices.text: were unable to master official narratives about the Second World War because alternative accounts had displaced them

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: citizens 'can recite the narrative fluently while remaining emotionally detached or even privately skeptical' — high mastery without appropriation. C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: This inverts the relationship: the passage says citizens master without appropriating, not that they appropriate while publicly questioning.
explanations.B: The passage does not mention family memory as an alternative; it describes private skepticism, not an alternative account.
explanations.D: The passage's entire point about post-Soviet Russia is the split between mastery and appropriation — finding both would contradict the passage's claim.
explanations.E: The passage says citizens can 'recite the narrative fluently' — they have mastered it; they have not been displaced from it.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of survey research in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: criticize quantitative social science as inherently inferior to ethnographic methods for studying historical memory

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate a specific methodological risk that follows from Wertsch's mastery-appropriation distinction, particularly in certain political contexts

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a new argument about the limitations of social science that the passage then develops in detail

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede a limitation in Wertsch's framework by noting that it cannot be confirmed through standard survey instruments

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that Halbwachs's original framework anticipated the problems with survey-based measurement of social memory

explanations.correct: The final paragraph explicitly draws out the methodological consequence of Wertsch's mastery-appropriation distinction for survey research, and specifies that the risk is 'with particular force in authoritarian or post-authoritarian contexts' — exactly what B describes.
explanations.A: The passage does not declare quantitative methods 'inherently inferior'; it identifies a specific limitation relevant to Wertsch's distinction, not a general condemnation.
explanations.C: Survey research is introduced as a consequence of Wertsch's framework, not as a new independent argument; and the passage does not develop it further beyond the paragraph.
explanations.D: The passage implies that survey research fails to capture appropriation, but frames this as a warning to researchers, not as a limitation in Wertsch's framework itself.
explanations.E: Halbwachs is not mentioned in the final paragraph; attributing this anticipation to him is unsupported.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the distinction Wertsch draws between mastery and appropriation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A student memorizes a patriotic anthem for a school ceremony but privately regards the historical claims embedded in its lyrics as exaggerated or false.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historian rewrites a national founding narrative to incorporate the perspectives of previously marginalized groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A community erects a monument to a local battle, thereby converting a living tradition into a formalized site of commemoration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government archives official documents from a former regime so that future historians can scrutinize its record.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A sociologist conducts fieldwork among members of a diaspora community to understand how they reconstruct memories of their homeland.

explanations.correct: Mastery = ability to reproduce a narrative accurately; appropriation = internalizing it as genuinely one's own. A student who can perform the anthem accurately but privately doubts its claims has achieved mastery without appropriation — the core distinction Wertsch draws.
explanations.B: This describes historiographical revision, which is about changing the narrative itself, not the distinction between reproducing and internalizing a given narrative.
explanations.C: This describes Nora's concept of lieux de mémoire — converting living tradition into institutional commemoration — not Wertsch's mastery-appropriation distinction.
explanations.D: Archiving is another instantiation of Nora's sites-of-memory concept; it has no bearing on the individual psychological distinction Wertsch draws.
explanations.E: Diaspora memory reconstruction is an interesting social-memory phenomenon, but it does not specifically illustrate the mastery-without-appropriation split.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Wertsch's claim that mastery and appropriation are genuinely distinct psychological states?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individuals who score high on tests of historical knowledge also tend to express higher levels of national pride in anonymous surveys.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In longitudinal studies, citizens who could accurately recall official national narratives in their youth were no more likely than others to act in ways consistent with those narratives in later life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments in authoritarian states invest heavily in educational programs designed to teach official historical narratives to students.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Survey research has been shown to be reliable in measuring factual knowledge about historical events in liberal democratic societies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The narratives that citizens most readily recall are those that were introduced during early childhood education.

explanations.correct: If citizens who master official narratives do not behave in ways those narratives would predict — that is, if narrative mastery does not translate into the values and dispositions that appropriation would produce — this provides direct behavioral evidence that mastery and appropriation are distinct and separable states.
explanations.A: A positive correlation between knowledge test scores and national pride would actually suggest that mastery and appropriation tend to go together, weakening rather than strengthening Wertsch's distinction.
explanations.C: Government investment in educational programs is consistent with Wertsch's framework but does not distinguish mastery from appropriation — it only speaks to efforts to produce mastery.
explanations.D: The reliability of surveys in liberal democracies is irrelevant to whether mastery and appropriation are distinct; the passage's concern is specifically with contexts where performance is socially mandatory.
explanations.E: Early childhood retention speaks to the robustness of mastery but says nothing about whether the narrative is appropriated as one's own.
